body.spec:
THE PIECE THAT MAKES PUSH REAL. A Claude Code CHANNEL is an MCP server named in `--channels`
that pushes events into the open session. Ours bridges the taskops board:

    board write (comment/assign/status) -> taskops ui WS (/api/live) -> server.ts
        -> channel event into the session ; and a `reply` tool -> POST /api/comment back.

STUDY FIRST (mandatory, in this order):
  1. ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/claude-plugins-official/external_plugins/fakechat/server.ts
     — the de-facto spec: how a channel registers, the event shape, the reply tool.
  2. WebFetch https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference — the protocol contract.
Copy the CONTRACT, not the chat UI.

DESIGN:
  - Bun + TypeScript, in plugin/channel/. This is a PLUGIN artifact, not part of the Python
    package — the zero-deps rule of the wheel is untouched.
  - server.ts on startup: if the taskops ui is not already listening on TASKOPS_UI_PORT
    (default 2140), SPAWN `taskops ui --port <port>` as a child and kill it on exit — the UI
    and the channel are ONE lifecycle, which answers "does the webserver start with the
    plugin": with the channel, yes.
  - subscribe to ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/live; forward INTO the session only what a person
    would want to interrupt for: comments mentioning a dev or the orchestrator, assignee set,
    status changes to review/blocked/done, lease-expiry recoveries. Heartbeats and activity
    NEVER cross — a channel that relays keystrokes trains the user to ignore it.
  - tools: `reply` (posts a comment to a card: args card, text) and `board` (returns the
    compact board snapshot). Nothing that spends money.
  - filtering config via env: TASKOPS_CHANNEL_EVENTS (csv of kinds), default the curated set.

HONEST LIMITS to state in plugin/channel/README.md: research preview; a custom channel needs
`claude --dangerously-load-development-channels ./plugin/channel` (verify exact syntax in the
reference doc and WRITE IT DOWN); anyone allowed to write the channel can approve permissions
if relay is declared — do NOT declare permission relay.

TESTS: bun is available (1.3.11). Python-side test_channel_contract.py asserts the WS side it
consumes exists (api/live serves events; /api/comment accepts the shape reply sends) — the
contract test that keeps Python honest about what TS depends on. For server.ts itself add
`bun test` files next to it (parse/filter logic factored into functions, tested without a
socket). Run both and paste output.

body.spec:
THE HOLE, REPRODUCED. In a fresh repo:

    next_task(task=t, actor="agent:t/uno")            # uno holds the lease
    update(t, status="released", actor="dev:otro")    # -> the card is `ready` again

Anybody can release anybody's lease. Found in a live log while diagnosing something else: a
sub-agent that could not claim a card went on to RELEASE the lease another actor was holding,
and the board looked fine afterwards — which is the worst shape a bug like this can have,
because the only trace is that somebody's work silently stopped being theirs.

Why it matters more than it reads: the lease is the ONE mechanism that stops two agents doing
the same card. A release anybody can call is a lock anybody can pick. Two agents, one card,
both convinced they hold it, both committing to the same branch.

WHAT TO BUILD.

(1) `released` requires the lease, or a dev's deliberate override. The rule:
      - the lease HOLDER may always release (that is the honest hand-back this exists for);
      - a `dev:` actor may release somebody else's, because a human unsticking a dead agent is
        a real and necessary act — but it must be RECORDED as what it is (the event body
        carries who was holding it, so a report can show "dev:berna took tk-x off
        agent:ana/w1");
      - any OTHER agent is REFUSED, naming the holder and pointing at `taskops_recover` for a
        worker that has actually gone silent.
    Home: the state machine (`engine/machine.py` / `engine/_review.py`'s neighbourhood), not
    the transport — every surface must get the same answer.

(2) Check the SAME question for every other transition that ends somebody's hold:
    `cancelled`, and `blocked`. If `cancelled` by a third party is also unguarded, decide
    deliberately: a dev cancelling a card somebody holds is legitimate; another agent doing it
    is the same hole with a different verb. Whatever is decided, TEST it.

(3) `taskops recover` must keep working — it is the sanctioned way to release a lapsed lease
    and it runs as whoever typed it. It already checks the heartbeat rather than the actor, so
    it should pass the new guard by construction; if it does not, the guard is wrong, not
    recover.

TESTS (tests/e2e or tests/engine, wherever the state machine's live):
  - holder releases -> allowed
  - another AGENT releases -> refused, message names the holder and taskops_recover
  - a dev releases -> allowed, and the event records the previous holder
  - recover still releases a silent worker's card
  - a card with NO lease is unaffected (releasing an unheld card stays whatever it is today)

Start with megabrain_grep naming: update status released, check_move Facts machine, leases
held_by take_lease, recover grace heartbeat.
body.title: a lease anybody can release is not a lease

body.spec:
FOUR TIMES NOW a specialist has failed for the same reason: it did not pass `actor=` on a
taskops call, resolved to the developer's `dev:<name>`, and was refused its own card. Each
time the answer was to write the instruction somewhere new — the delegation message, the
refusal text, the agent prompt. It keeps working for one call and dissolving by the third.
**An instruction is not a mechanism.** This card makes the identity travel.

TWO LEVERS, and the card wants BOTH because they cover different holes.

(1) `$TASKOPS_ACTOR` already exists and is already read (`engine.identity`, used by dispatched
    workers). It is the mechanism; nothing sets it for a sub-agent spawned by a host session.
    Make the MCP surface honour it as the DEFAULT when a call omits `actor` — check what
    `_project.caller` does today: if it already prefers the env var, then the gap is only that
    nobody sets it, and the fix is documentation plus (2). Verify before changing.

(2) DERIVE IT FROM THE CARD. When a call names a task (`next`, `update`, `capture` on an
    existing card) and omits `actor`, and that card has an `assignee`, the assignee IS the
    caller — a card assigned to `agent:me/api` being worked on has exactly one honest actor.
    This is the lever that needs no environment and no memory.
    GUARD IT CAREFULLY, because this is an identity inference and those go wrong quietly:
      - only when `actor` is ABSENT, never overriding a stated one;
      - only when the assignee is an `agent:` id (never impersonate a `dev:`);
      - only for the ASSIGNED card, never for a pool call;
      - and RECORD that it was inferred (a field on the event), so a reader can tell a claim
        the agent made from one taskops attributed to it.
    If any of those is uncomfortable, say so in the report rather than shipping it: a wrong
    inference here writes somebody else's name on work.

TESTS: an update with no actor on an assigned card is attributed to the assignee and says so;
with an explicit actor, the explicit one wins; a pool call with no actor still resolves to the
developer as today; a `dev:` assignee is never inferred; and the whole existing suite passes,
because every current caller passes an actor and must be unaffected.

Start with megabrain_grep naming: caller _project heartbeat, ENV_ACTOR identity parse,
arguments.optional actor, next_task update capture actor.
body.title: the actor is a mechanism, not an instruction

body.spec:
THE ASK, exactly: a card carries its REVIEWER, set when it is created. Two kinds:

    reviewer: dev:berna      a person closes it — the session must NOT
    reviewer: tester         a specialist closes it — spawn that agent
    reviewer: (empty)        the project default, then the stock verifier

WHERE IT LIVES. A field on the card, like `assignee` — settable by `tasks add`, `tasks edit`,
and `taskops_plan`'s entries. NOT a label: a label is a routing hint and this is a policy about
who may close, which is a different kind of fact and must not be diluted by a `labels` list
somebody edits for search.

VALIDATION, same shape as the assign endpoint already uses: a bare name must be a registered
agent (`.claude/agents/*.md`) and is refused with the known names when it is not; `dev:*` and
full `agent:<dev>/<name>` ids pass. `human` is accepted as a synonym for "whoever is reading
the board" and stored as such — it is what somebody will type.

THE DEFAULT is a project decision, so it belongs in the context layer, not in a constant:
`taskops context decision "reviewer: tester"` — read it, fall back to the stock verifier when
absent. Look at how `usecases/context.py` exposes facts before inventing a second mechanism.

ENFORCEMENT, and this is the half that makes it real rather than a note:
  - a card whose reviewer is a `dev:` (or `human`) REFUSES `done` from any agent, with a
    sentence naming who is expected — the existing review guard already refuses the agent that
    entered review; this widens it to "the reviewer this card names".
  - a card whose reviewer is an agent keeps today's rule (anyone but the one who entered
    review; a dev may always close).
  - a card with no criteria and no reviewer behaves exactly as it does today. REGRESSION GUARD,
    test it.

Show it where it is decided: `tasks show` and the card panel display the reviewer.

Start with megabrain_grep naming: Task assignee contracts, plan _entry fields, edit EDITABLE_FIELDS,
_review closing entered_review_by, agents registry agent_named.

implemented, tested 4/4, committed, moved to review, and the card sat there.

The line must ROUTE, the same way the assignment line already does:

  reviewer is an AGENT  -> "tk-b61984 is in review, reviewed by `tester`. Spawn a `tester`
                           sub-agent on it (actor=agent:<dev>/tester): read the card's
                           acceptance criteria and the diff on <branch>, run the tests, then
                           close it with evidence or send it back with findings."

  reviewer is a HUMAN   -> "tk-b61984 NEEDS A HUMAN REVIEW (<who>). Do not close it and do not
                           review it yourself. Commit <sha> on <branch>. <n> criteria. Open
                           <board-url>/#<card>." — and the session is expected to stop there.

  no reviewer           -> today's default, stated: the stock verifier.

The event body already carries what the line needs (`to`, `from`, the actor); the reviewer has
to come from the CARD, so the channel needs one read — use the board endpoint it already
speaks to rather than inventing a second client.

Keep the pure/impure split this module has: routing decided in a tested function, the fetch in
server.ts. Tests for all three branches plus the regression: a status event that is not
`review` is unchanged.

A CHAT WITH THE SESSION, reachable from anywhere in the board — a sidebar that slides in over
whatever you are looking at, not a fourth tab. Berna asked for exactly this after being shown
the per-card Reply box: "algo que se dispare en cualquier página y se abra en un sidebar con
animation".

WHY IT IS NOT A TAB: a tab is a place you GO, and this is a thing you say while you are looking
at something else — usually about the very card on screen. Making it a destination would mean
losing your place to ask a question about it.

THE SURFACE
  - A trigger present in EVERY view (Board, Activity, Reports): a button in the header, plus a
    keyboard shortcut. Pick one that cannot collide with typing in the reply box or the search
    field — check what the UI already binds before choosing, and make Escape close it.
  - Slides in from the right over the content, does not reflow the board underneath. Animated:
    a transform+opacity transition, ~150-200ms, and it must respect
    `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` by appearing without the slide.
  - Persists across tab switches and page state: opening it on Reports and switching to Board
    leaves it open, with its scroll position.
  - Shows the conversation newest-at-the-bottom, an input at the foot, and — when the board is
    on a card — a one-line hint that the message will carry that card's id as context.
  - A dot on the trigger when something arrived while it was closed. Cleared on open.

WHERE THE MESSAGES LIVE. Events, like everything else — do NOT invent a store. A chat message
is not about a card, so it needs a home: `usecases/context.py` already files project-wide facts
under a sentinel task (`CONTEXT_TASK = "project"`), and that is the precedent to follow, with a
new kind (`chat`). Read that module before designing this; if the sentinel turns out to be the
wrong home, say why in the report rather than quietly inventing a table.
  - It replicates like everything else, which means a teammate SEES the conversation. That is a
    feature (the reasoning survives) and a hazard (people write things in a chat box they would
    not commit). Say which one you chose in the docstring, and if messages should be
    LOCAL_ONLY_KINDS instead, argue it — do not decide it silently.

THE ROUND TRIP, and this is the half that makes it more than a notes field:
  - Posting a chat message emits an event -> `/api/live` -> `plugin/channel/server.ts` already
    tails that feed -> it reaches the open Claude Code session as a channel message. The channel
    filter must SELECT the new kind (it is in `plugin/channel/events.ts`, `classify`); that file
    belongs to another agent right now, so DO NOT EDIT IT — write down the exact one-line change
    needed and report it.
  - The session answers with the channel's `reply` tool, which today posts a COMMENT ON A CARD.
    A chat reply has no card. Report what `reply` would need (a `chat: true`, or a `card` that
    may be omitted) — again, do not edit that file.
  - So this card ships the board half end to end and NAMES the two lines the channel needs. The
    conversation works one-way (you -> session) the moment this lands, and both ways when those
    two lines are applied.

the same policy as `/api/comment` — assert the 401 and the `--readonly` 403 in tests, like
`assigning.py` does. The feed already broadcasts anything `record()` writes; verify it rather
than adding a parallel notification, and if it does not, fix THAT.

are the siblings to copy. No new colour, no new radius, no bold. Rebuild the committed bundle
(`cd ui && npm run build`) and commit it, as the assign card did.

THE REFERENCE, study it first (megabrain has ~/pinecall/webrtc indexed):
  - `src/widget/ChatView.tsx` L56-105 `StreamingText` — the rAF character reveal over markdown

Copy the PATTERN (reveal budget per frame, cancel on unmount, render markdown of the revealed
prefix), not the code. The board already has `ui/src/components/Markdown.tsx` — use it, do not
add a markdown dependency.

FOUR PIECES.

(1) MARKDOWN + REVEAL. A session reply (`body.source == "session"`) renders as markdown and

    history render instantly and completely — replaying the animation on every open would make
    the sidebar feel broken. Respect prefers-reduced-motion: full text at once.

(2) THINKING. After you send, the session is working and the sidebar says so — a quiet
    "thinking…" row (the pinecall indicator pattern) that appears when a board-sourced message
    is sent and clears when EITHER a session reply arrives OR an `activity` event does (the
    agent is working — show what it is doing instead). Cap it: if nothing arrives in ~90s, the
    row fades to "still working — or the session is closed", because a spinner that lies
    forever teaches people to ignore it. The channel may genuinely not be running.

(3) THE TOOL STRIP. `activity` events already carry "the tool, and the file or command it
    touched" (hooks record them via track()); they reach the same socket the chat listens to.
    Render them as a compact live strip under the thread — one line per call, tool name as a
    chip, target truncated middle-out, newest at the bottom, auto-scrolled, capped to the last
    ~50 with a "· · ·" above when truncated. This is observability, not conversation: dimmer
    than messages, collapsible, and its arrival must NOT clear the unread dot or count as a
    reply. VERIFY the events actually reach the feed before styling anything: post one by hand
    (usecases track()) and watch /api/live.

    /Users/berna/experiments/fake-project/.claude/settings.json (project-level hooks are a
    Claude Code feature) so Berna's next session emits real activity. Document that step in
    the chat section of docs/agents.md — one paragraph.

(4) THE LEAK. Known Claude Code bug (anthropics/claude-code #66011, #68615): tool-call markup

    TRAILING fragments matching closing tool-markup tags (`</parameter>`, `</invoke>`,
    `</function_...>` and orphan opening `<invoke ...>` tails) from the END of the text only —
    never touch the middle, where somebody may legitimately be quoting XML. Pure function in
    events.ts, bun-tested with the exact string Berna received. Link both issues in a comment.

`tasks edit --milestone <id>` + el campo en el verbo rpc `edit`. `milestone` entra a EDITABLE_FIELDS y viaja por el camino que ya existía (un evento `edited` por campo, arbitración por timestamp, UPDATE con whitelist) — no un segundo camino de escritura para una columna.

LA DECISIÓN QUE VALE: la validación NO es la de `plan`, es la de `--carry`. `plan` con un id explícito acepta cualquier capítulo que exista; mover trabajo que YA existe sólo puede apuntar a un capítulo ACTIVO, porque una card abierta dentro de un capítulo alcanzado es una de dos mentiras. Y no se puede vaciar (`--milestone ""` refusado): una card pertenece a exactamente uno, así que "sin capítulo" no es un estado que alguien pida — es la forma en que llega una card escrita antes de que los capítulos existieran. El guard vive en `_planinto`, que ya era el dueño de esa pregunta; una copia del lookup en `edit` era la otra opción y era la mala.

MCP NO lo lleva y el spec pedía que sí: no existe tool de edición de cards en MCP, y es a propósito (está escrito en USAGE.md) — un agente que puede reescribir su propio spec puede convencerse de haber terminado. Así que el spec de esta card pedía un sitio que no existe; lo dejo afuera y lo digo.

MUTADO: (1) saqué el chequeo de activo → el refusal del capítulo cerrado no salta, test falla; (2) saqué `milestone` de EDITABLE_FIELDS → la adopción y el movimiento fallan los dos con "`milestone` is not editable".
